lesson.title: Trading TCP for QUIC: How HTTP/3 Finishes the Job
lesson.summary: HTTP/3 keeps HTTP/2's idea of multiplexed streams but moves them onto QUIC, a transport protocol built on UDP, which removes the transport layer head of line blocking that HTTP/2 could not avoid.
lesson.body:
HTTP/2 fixed head of line blocking within HTTP but left a version of the same problem sitting one layer down, in TCP itself. Since every multiplexed stream in HTTP/2 shares one TCP connection, and TCP insists on delivering bytes to the application in the exact order they were sent, a single lost packet anywhere in that connection stalls delivery of every stream until the missing data is retransmitted and TCP can restore the correct order. HTTP/3 addresses this by changing the transport underneath HTTP entirely.

Instead of running over TCP, HTTP/3 runs over QUIC, a transport protocol built on top of UDP. UDP by itself gives no ordering or reliability guarantees at all, which is exactly why QUIC exists: it adds reliability, congestion control, and encryption back in, but it does so per stream rather than per connection. QUIC multiplexes independent streams natively at the transport layer, and loss recovery is scoped to the individual stream that lost a packet. If a packet carrying part of one stream's data goes missing, only that stream pauses to wait for retransmission; every other stream sharing the same QUIC connection keeps delivering data to the application without interruption. This is the key improvement HTTP/3 delivers over HTTP/2: it does not just avoid head of line blocking in HTTP, it avoids it in the transport layer too.

QUIC brings a few other practical advantages along with it. It integrates the TLS 1.3 handshake directly into the transport handshake, so establishing a new, encrypted QUIC connection typically takes fewer round trips than establishing a TCP connection and then layering TLS on top of it separately, and a returning client can often send data immediately on the first flight in what is called zero round trip mode. QUIC connections are also identified by a connection ID rather than by the client's IP address and port, which means a connection can survive a network change, like a phone switching from Wi-Fi to cellular data, without having to be torn down and reestablished.

HTTP/3 keeps the semantics that HTTP/2 introduced, multiplexed streams and compressed headers, adapting header compression into a variant called QPACK designed to work with QUIC's stream model instead of HPACK's. Consider the same page load used to illustrate HTTP/2, with a dozen or so resources requested over one connection. Under HTTP/2 over TCP, a single lost packet anywhere in that connection stalls all of those in flight responses until it is retransmitted. Under HTTP/3 over QUIC, only the one stream that happened to lose a packet pauses; the rest keep streaming in normally, and the page keeps rendering. That difference, invisible in ideal network conditions but very real on lossy mobile or Wi-Fi connections, is the whole point of moving from TCP to QUIC.
